520	Because what happens, again, is that Onkelos usually translates

521	word for word, a literal translation. There are a few

522	places in the Torah where he does not translate literally,

523	but departs from his custom and gives a

524	translation by meaning,

525	not literal. This verse is one

527	The Targum of course translates this into Aramaic. "Helped."

528	Not everyone here is a professional Aramaic speaker, since it is

529	not a language people actually speak today. I'll show

531	into the holy tongue, and then you can see the difference.

536	Adam." The languages are very, very similar.

537	For example, instead of the word "vayyitzer" it says "uvara," creation.

538	So creation, formation: to many people these seem like

539	synonyms, and that is how he translates it. "And HaShem Elokim

540	created the man." Very interesting, note

541	that the letter aleph in Hebrew is replaced by yod

542	in Aramaic: "yat Adam," "et ha-Adam." "Yat Adam." The following words

543	are very similar: "dust from the ground." What is the translation?

544	"Afra min adamta," that is, exactly the same word with an aleph

545	at the end. "Afra min adamta." Up to here it is a

546	literal translation, a Hebrew word against an

547	Aramaic word. Moving on: "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Onkelos

548	translates "vayipach"

549	as "He blew." The Holy One, blessed be He, blew, "be-apo," "be-anpohi."

550	Again, the letters "apo" are found within the Aramaic word

551	"be-anpohi," with the addition of

552	the heh and the nun, "be-anpohi."

553	Okay, "nishmat chayim," Onkelos translates "nishmeta," right?

554	Again this characteristic aleph, like "afra min adamta."

555	So "nishmeta," instead of

556	"nishmat chayim,"

557	"de-chaya": he adds a dalet here. "Chaya" is "chayim," "de-chaya," of

559	"And He blew into his nostrils a soul of life." Now comes the change.
